section_summary: This section concludes a broad assessment of Japan’s 1940 economy and 1941 outlook, covering raw silk, rice, foreign trade, mobilization, shortages, and the risks posed by dependence on imported resources. It then assembles wartime intelligence on Japanese labor, food rationing, agricultural output, and strategic preparedness, including a lengthy study arguing that Japan had accumulated substantial oil and mineral reserves but remained vulnerable in iron ore. The final pages contain cross-reference and routing sheets plus a Tokyo Embassy despatch enclosing translations of Japanese financial, banking, and machine-tool regulations issued in late 1941.

subfiles.title: Annual Economic Review of Japan, 1940, and Outlook for 1941 (continuation)
subfiles.about: Continuation of an economic survey discussing raw silk, rice, foreign trade, and Japan’s prospects for 1941.
subfiles.summary: The report records falling raw-silk prices and exports, rice shortages, government purchasing and distribution controls, and greater reliance on imports from China and Southeast Asia. It describes record nominal foreign trade but a weakened export balance, growing dependence on the yen bloc, and efforts to replace lost European markets. Its outlook anticipates tighter shortages, financial strain, worsening agricultural conditions, and increasingly dangerous relations with the United States and Great Britain, while warning that collapse was not necessarily imminent.

subfiles.title: Charge Slip for File 894.50
subfiles.about: Administrative form recording the later charging or circulation of material from file 894.50.
subfiles.summary: The sheet contains file and charge information, clerical initials, and a September 14, 1943 notation. Much of the handwriting is illegible and appears unrelated to the substantive economic records.

subfiles.title: Economic Interests Item No. 99: Japanese Toy Sales in Mexico
subfiles.about: Reports Mexican resistance to Japanese toys and a possible low-price purchase of measuring tapes.
subfiles.summary: Curt Gestefeld states that Japanese toys have little market in Mexico because clients resent Japanese firms bypassing import agents after learning which products sell. Dibaco might purchase metric measuring tapes, but only cheaply because superior Swiss products were available. The page bears a January 1942 receipt marking.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Note to Mr. Acheson on Japanese Labor and Food Reports
subfiles.about: Calls attention to reports on Japanese occupational labor distribution and food rationing.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies two transmitted papers, one containing occupational-distribution tables and the other covering food rationing in Japan. It remarks that rationing does not appear especially severe and that the study concludes Japan could remain self-sufficient for at least three years.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2416 Forwarding Ministry of Economic Warfare Material on Japan
subfiles.from: Harold Shantz, for the Ambassador, United States Embassy, London
subfiles.about: Forwards British Ministry of Economic Warfare papers on Japanese labor distribution and food rationing.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy transmits two papers received from the Ministry of Economic Warfare as a follow-up to Despatch No. 2195. Although similar information was probably already available in Washington, the papers demonstrated the Ministry’s areas of interest. A Ministry official also requested any corresponding information that United States authorities could supply.

subfiles.title: Occupational Distribution of Labour in Japan (Proper) in the Summer of 1941
subfiles.about: Estimates Japan’s 1941 workforce by occupation and industrial branch using census data and factory-employment sampling.
subfiles.summary: The paper compares estimated 1941 employment with the 1930 census, showing growth in industry, mining, civil service, and especially the armed forces. It explains the assumptions used to estimate workers in factories, workshops, construction, and other industrial branches. Tables place the occupied workforce at about 35.25 million out of a population of 73.9 million.

subfiles.title: Food Rationing in Japan
subfiles.from: Ministry of Economic Warfare, Enemy Resources Department (Japan)
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese food and fuel rations and evaluates the country’s prospective food self-sufficiency.
subfiles.summary: The report lists ration levels for rice, food oil, charcoal, wheat flour, sugar, and matches in six major cities, while noting that meat, fish, vegetables, and canned foods were not generally rationed. It explains ration-card administration and the creation of a Foodstuffs Distribution Committee. The assessment concludes that imports from Indochina and Thailand, fish supplies, and Manchukuo soybeans could sustain Japan for at least three years, while a supplementary note discusses compulsory grain mixing and restrictions on rice polishing.

subfiles.title: Department of Justice Letter Transmitting Information on Japanese Resources
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Department of Justice
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle, Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits a confidential-source memorandum on selected Japanese resources.
subfiles.summary: The letter encloses a memorandum dated December 22, 1941, based on information received from an outside confidential source. Copies were also directed to naval and War Department intelligence officials.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese Labor and Grain Resources
subfiles.about: Provides fragmentary estimates of labor availability and Japanese rice, wheat, barley, and oat supplies.
subfiles.summary: The surviving text says unskilled labor was plentiful in Manchukuo and Korea but skilled workers were scarce and needed for supervision and training. It gives estimates for rice carryover, the 1941 rice crop, per-capita rice consumption, and the wheat, barley, and oat crops. The OCR begins mid-sentence, so part of the memorandum is evidently missing or unreadable.

subfiles.title: Letter Sending a Study of Japan’s Economic Preparedness
subfiles.about: Sends Rosden’s paper on Japan’s economic preparedness to the Department of State.
subfiles.summary: Rosden offers Herbert Feis a copy of his study in view of Feis’s official responsibilities for international economic affairs. The letter serves as the covering communication for the paper beginning on the next page.

subfiles.title: Extent and Limitations of Japan’s Economic Preparedness
subfiles.about: Assesses whether Japan possessed the industrial capacity, stockpiles, and strategic resources needed for a prolonged war.
subfiles.summary: Rosden argues that Japan adopted a long-term economic war plan in the 1930s based on stockpiling, synthetic production, industrial expansion, and territorial conquest. Detailed estimates cover petroleum, aluminum, tungsten, tin, rubber, copper, manganese, scrap iron, pig iron, steel, and iron ore. He concludes that Japan had accumulated enough oil and most other materials for several years but remained dependent on Malaya and the Philippines for the iron ore needed to sustain expanded steel production. The study therefore treats Allied control of those territories and sea communications as the key to Japan’s economic defeat.

subfiles.title: Reply Thanking George E. Rosden for His Study
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Rosden’s study on Japanese economic preparedness.
subfiles.summary: Feis thanks Rosden for sending the Department a copy of his study. He states that it will be read with interest.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note: Economic Situation in Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a Shanghai despatch reporting Shudo’s comments on worsening Japanese shortages.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references Despatch No. 829 concerning the increasing seriousness of Japan’s economic situation. It specifically identifies shortages of raw materials and foodstuffs and directs readers to file 894.00/1154 for the original.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note: Japanese Raw-Material Gains in Indochina and Thailand
subfiles.about: References a report and chart on raw materials gained by Japan in Indochina and Thailand.
subfiles.summary: The sheet describes a paper analyzing Japan’s acquisition of raw materials in Indochina and Thailand, accompanied by a chart locating their sources. It directs readers to Military Attaché Report No. 47978 in file 894.24/1859.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note: Economic Information in Japanese Broadcasts
subfiles.about: References a telegram requesting reports on economic information contained in Japanese broadcasts.
subfiles.summary: The note records a request for reporting on all economic information that could be obtained from Japanese broadcasts. It points to Telegram No. 666, sent at 9 p.m., in file 894.76/83a.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Service Routing Sheet
subfiles.about: Administrative routing form for classified material circulated through War Department intelligence offices.
subfiles.summary: The form lists Military Intelligence Service groups, branches, and possible actions, including information, reply preparation, and courier delivery. A handwritten instruction indicates that the report must be returned to the State Department through a contact section by December 10.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Group Routing Sheet
subfiles.from: Far Eastern Group, Military Intelligence Service
subfiles.about: Internal routing form distributing material among intelligence branches and sections.
subfiles.summary: The sheet lists Far Eastern Group recipients and other Military Intelligence Service components, with options for information, action, filing, or return. A short handwritten remark is largely illegible.

subfiles.title: Despatch Transmitting Materials Prepared for Financial and Economic Reports
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits seven items prepared before December 8, 1941, for the Commercial Attaché’s regular financial and economic reports.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards regulatory and statistical materials that had been prepared as enclosures to the Commercial Attaché’s reports before the outbreak of war. The enclosure list covers postal savings, bank capital controls, bank statistics, machine-tool regulation, price controls, and rules governing aliens in the Japanese-mandated South Sea Islands. The despatch specifies the distribution of originals, copies, and hectograph copies.

subfiles.title: Revision in Rate of Interest on Postal Savings Money
subfiles.about: Translation of Imperial Ordinance No. 990 revising interest rates for Japanese postal savings.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance sets ordinary postal-savings interest at 2.76 percent, with higher rates in Korea, Taiwan, the Kwantung Leased Territory, Sakhalin, and the South Sea Islands. It specifies rates for fixed-term, collection-system, and transfer-account savings and permits reduced interest on large balances. The rules were to take effect on December 1, 1941, with transitional protection for certain existing deposits.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Copy: Revision in Rate of Interest on Postal Savings Money
subfiles.about: A second copy of the translation revising Japanese postal-savings interest rates.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats Imperial Ordinance No. 990, including the regional and fixed-term savings rates. It also repeats the provisions for large deposits, transfer accounts, the December 1 enforcement date, and transitional treatment of existing collection-system savings.

subfiles.title: Revision in Enforcement Regulations for Ordinance Pertaining to Employment of Capital by Banks, Etc.
subfiles.from: Okinori Kaya, Hiroya Ino, Nobusuke Kishi, and Shigenori Togo
subfiles.about: Revises banking capital-control regulations by adding ministerially designated funds to exempt categories.
subfiles.summary: The joint ordinance adds a new category covering capital funds designated by the competent minister and adjusts the cross-reference in Article 8. The attached reference text lists loans and capital accommodations exempt from Articles 4–7, including government-directed finance, secured lending, call loans, loans to monetary institutions, and lending to local public bodies. It also explains how qualifying transactions are excluded from regulatory loan and overdraft calculations.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Copy: Revision in Enforcement Regulations for Employment of Capital by Banks
subfiles.from: Okinori Kaya, Hiroya Ino, Nobusuke Kishi, and Shigenori Togo
subfiles.about: A second copy of the joint ordinance revising bank capital-employment regulations.
subfiles.summary: The copy repeats the new provision permitting designation of additional capital funds by the competent minister. Its reference section again enumerates exempt forms of government-directed, secured, short-term, institutional, and municipal lending and their treatment in regulatory calculations.

subfiles.title: Designation of Capital Funds under Article 8 of the Bank Capital Regulations
subfiles.from: Okinori Kaya, Hiroya Ino, Nobusuke Kishi, and Shigenori Togo
subfiles.about: Designates munitions-bill finance and export-loss purchasing finance as qualifying capital funds.
subfiles.summary: The notice designates capital supplied through the discount of munitions bills drawn on and accepted by the Japan Industrial Bank under the National General Mobilization Law. It also covers purchasing capital supplied to purchasing organs under the loss-compensation system for suspended exports.

subfiles.title: Bank Deposits, Loans, and Security Holdings at the End of October 1941
subfiles.about: Tabulates deposits, loans, and securities of Japanese banks at the end of October 1941.
subfiles.summary: The table presents figures in thousands of yen for the Bank of Japan, ordinary banks, savings banks, special banks, and government deposits. It compares October totals with September 1941 and October 1940, showing substantial year-over-year growth in deposits, loans, and security holdings despite several OCR-damaged entries.

subfiles.title: Revision in Ordinance Pertaining to Enforcement of the Machine Tool Manufacturing Industry Law
subfiles.from: Hideki Tojo, Shigetaro Shimada, Okinori Kaya, and Nobusuke Kishi
subfiles.about: Revises enforcement rules governing Japanese machine-tool manufacturers, taxation, compulsory transfers, compensation, and industrial reserves.
subfiles.summary: Imperial Ordinance No. 989 changes the production-scale thresholds and terminology applying to machine-tool enterprises and sets procedures for calculating capital and claiming tax exemptions. It regulates compensation for losses arising from government orders, negotiations and adjudication over factory or equipment transfers, assignment and rental prices, deposits, and passage of ownership or lease rights. Further provisions govern publication of decisions, accelerated depreciation, and reserve funds for research, equipment expansion, and technical improvement. The final page begins a reference extract from the earlier 1938 enforcement ordinance and ends mid-provision.
